content: In human anatomy, the wrist is the flexible and narrower connection between the forearm and the palm. It is composed of a double row of small, short bones known as carpals, which are interlocked to form a pliable hinge-like structure. The wrist joint, also referred to as the radiocarpal articulation, is a condyloid joint that allows for three degrees of freedom in movement. Structure of the Joint The wrist joint is formed by the lower end of the radius and the undersurface of the articular disk above, as well as the scaphoid, lunate, and triquetral bones below. The articular surface of the radius and the undersurface of the articular disk together create a transversely elliptical concave surface, known as the receiving cavity. The superior articular surfaces of the scaphoid, lunate, and triquetrum form a smooth convex surface, referred to as the condyle, which fits into the concavity. The bones of the wrist can be remembered using the mnemonic Some Lovers Try Positions That They Can't Handle, which corresponds to the following bones in order: Proximal row (radial to ulnar): Scaphoid, Lunate, Triquetral, Pisiform Distal row (radial to ulnar): Trapezium, Trapezoid, Capitate, Hamate Ligaments The wrist joint is enclosed by a capsule that is reinforced by several ligaments, including: The palmar radiocarpal ligament The dorsal radiocarpal ligament The ulnar collateral ligament (wrist) The radial collateral ligament (wrist) The synovial membrane lines the deep surfaces of these ligaments, extending from the margins of the lower end of the radius and the articular disk above to the margins of the articular surfaces of the carpal bones below. This membrane is loose and lax, with numerous folds, particularly on the posterior side. Movements The wrist joint permits a range of movements, including flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, and circumduction. These movements are studied in conjunction with those of the carpus, as they are functionally combined.
